questions.question: What is the difference between == and is in Python?
questions.title: == vs is in Python
questions.direct_answer: `==` asks whether two objects have equal values, using their equality rules. `is` asks whether both expressions refer to the exact same object; use it for intentional singleton checks such as `value is None`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand value equality, object identity, and why implementation reuse must not decide program behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `is` for strings or numbers because a small test happens to reuse the same object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that `==` may call `__eq__`, while identity cannot be overloaded and is the correct relationship for `None`.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Separate two questions that can look similar in a small test: whether values are equal and whether two names point to one object.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `==` compares values; `is` compares object identity.
Two different objects can be equal: separate `[1, 2]` lists compare equal but are not identical.
A class can customize `==` through `__eq__`; it cannot customize identity.
Use `value is None` and `value is not None` for the `None` singleton.
Never rely on string or integer interning for an identity comparison.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`==` compares values. It asks the objects' type whether the two values should count as equal: lists compare their elements, strings compare their text, and a user-defined class can implement `__eq__`. Equality can therefore describe domain meaning, such as two ticket objects having the same ticket code, even when they are separate objects.

`is` compares identity. It is true only when both expressions refer to the exact same object, and a class cannot redefine that relationship. After `alias = original`, `alias is original` is true because assignment creates another reference. Creating another object with equal contents does not give it the same identity.

If `a = [1, 2]` and `b = [1, 2]`, then `a == b` is true because the list elements match, while `a is b` is false because two lists were created. If `c = a`, then `c is a` is true. These results answer three different questions rather than contradicting one another.

Use `value is None` or `value is not None` because `None` is a singleton and the intended question is identity. This check also cannot be changed by a surprising custom `__eq__` method. For ordinary values such as names, IDs, amounts, strings, and lists, the intended relationship is normally equality, so use `==`.

A Python implementation may reuse some string or integer objects, so `is` can appear to work for a value comparison in a small test. That interning is an implementation detail and can vary with the value, runtime, or how the expression was created. Use `==` for equal meaning, `is` for one exact object, and `is None` for absence represented by the `None` singleton.

beats.spokenText: `==` compares values. Equality can therefore describe domain meaning, such as two ticket objects having the same ticket code, even when they are separate objects.

beats.spokenText: `is` compares identity. It is true only when both expressions refer to the exact same object, and a class cannot redefine that relationship. After `alias = original`, `alias is original` is true because assignment creates another reference. Creating another object with equal contents does not give it the same identity.

This check also cannot be changed by a surprising custom `__eq__` method. For ordinary values such as names, IDs, amounts, strings, and lists, the intended relationship is normally equality, so use `==`.

support.title: Custom equality does not change identity
support.code:
class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, code):
        self.code = code

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Ticket) and self.code == other.code

first = Ticket("A17")
second = Ticket("A17")
print(first == second)
print(first is second)

result = None
print(result is None)
support.caption: The tickets are equal by their code but remain different objects; `None` uses the identity relationship.

beats.cue: Reject implementation reuse as application logic
beats.spokenText: A Python implementation may reuse some string or integer objects, so `is` can appear to work for a value comparison in a small test. That interning is an implementation detail and can vary with the value, runtime, or how the expression was created. Use `==` for equal meaning, `is` for one exact object, and `is None` for absence represented by the `None` singleton.
beats.recallRule: Use `==` for equal values and `is` only when object identity is the relationship you actually mean.

sections.title: Value and identity are different relationships
sections.content:
Every Python object has an identity, a type, and a value. Identity answers “which object is this?” while equality answers “should these values count as equal?”

Assignment does not copy an object by itself. After `alias = original`, both names refer to one object, so `alias is original` is true. Creating another list with the same elements produces a different identity, but list equality can still return true.

Equality dispatches to type behavior. An expression such as `left == right` can involve `__eq__` methods and may even return a non-Boolean result for specialized libraries. Identity is a fixed language relationship and always tests whether the references are the same.

sections.title: Names, objects, and comparisons
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[name a] --> L1["list object [1, 2]"]
  C[name c] --> L1
  B[name b] --> L2["another list object [1, 2]"]
  L1 -. equal elements .-> L2
```

`a is c` is true because both arrows end at one object. `a == b` is true because the two list values match, even though `a is b` is false.

sections.title: Choose the relationship
sections.content:
| Question you mean | Operator | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Do the values match? | `==` | `entered_name == saved_name` |
| Are these references the exact same object? | `is` | `cached is original` |
| Is the optional value absent? | `is None` | `result is None` |
| Is the optional value present? | `is not None` | `result is not None` |

sections.title: Run both comparisons
sections.content:
```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a

print(a == b)  # True: equal list values
print(a is b)  # False: two list objects
print(a is c)  # True: c aliases a

result = None
if result is None:
    print("No result")
```

Avoid `name is "Ada"` or `count is 100`. Object reuse can make those tests look stable even though identity is the wrong relationship.

sections.title: Check the intended meaning
sections.content: “The submitted status has the value `approved`” uses `==`. “No result was returned” uses `is None`. “This cache returned the very same object instance” uses `is`.

followup_questions: How can a custom `__eq__` method change the result of `==`?
Why is `value is None` preferred to `value == None`?
What is object interning, and why should application logic not depend on it?

questions.question: How does Python short-circuit Boolean AND and OR expressions?
questions.title: Python AND/OR Short-Circuit Evaluation
questions.direct_answer: `and` stops at the first false value, while `or` stops at the first true value. Each operator returns the selected operand itself, not necessarily `True` or `False`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know evaluation stops early and that Boolean operators return operands.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `value or default` when valid false values such as `0`, `False`, or an empty string must be preserved.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect short-circuiting to safe guards and distinguish absence from general falsiness.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Predict which operands run, which operand becomes the result, and when a concise fallback expression loses information.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `x and y` returns `x` when `x` is false; otherwise it evaluates and returns `y`.
`x or y` returns `x` when `x` is true; otherwise it evaluates and returns `y`.
The right operand is skipped when the left operand already decides the result.
The result is an operand, not automatically a Boolean value.
Use an explicit `is None` check when false values are valid data rather than missing data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python evaluates `x and y` from left to right. If `x` is false in a Boolean context, it returns `x` and never evaluates `y`. If `x` is true, it evaluates and returns `y`. In a longer chain, `and` returns the first false operand, or the final operand when all earlier values are true.

Python evaluates `x or y` in the opposite way. If `x` is true, it returns `x` and skips `y`; otherwise it evaluates and returns `y`. A fallback chain such as `configured_name or environment_name or "guest"` therefore returns the first true operand, or the final operand if none before it is true.

These operators select an operand; they do not automatically produce `True` or `False`. `"Ada" or "guest"` returns the string `"Ada"`, and `0 and expensive()` returns the integer `0` without calling the function. Use `bool(expression)` only when the consumer specifically requires a Boolean value.

Short-circuiting can guard an operation that is unsafe or unnecessary. `user is not None and user.get("active")` never reads from the dictionary when `user` is `None`. Keep visible side effects out of the skipped operand when their conditional execution would make the code harder to understand; an ordinary `if` is clearer in that case.

`None`, `False`, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers are all false in Boolean context. If zero is a valid timeout, `supplied or 30` incorrectly replaces it. Test `supplied is None` when only absence should use the default. The same distinction applies to empty cached results and explicit `False` settings.

sections.title: Boolean context selects an operand
sections.content:
Python first asks for the truth value of the left operand. A false built-in value includes `None`, `False`, numeric zero, and empty strings or containers. A user-defined object can participate through `__bool__`; if that is absent, a zero `__len__` also makes it false.

The operator then selects which expression's value becomes the result. This is why chained fallbacks work: `configured_name or environment_name or "guest"` returns the first true value. It is also why the pattern is wrong when an empty value has meaning.

Short-circuiting controls evaluation, not merely conversion. A function call on the skipped side never occurs.

sections.title: Evaluation paths
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Evaluate left operand] --> T{Is it true?}
  T -- Yes + `or` --> RO[Return left; skip right]
  T -- No + `or` --> EO[Evaluate and return right]
  T -- Yes + `and` --> EA[Evaluate and return right]
  T -- No + `and` --> RA[Return left; skip right]
```

sections.title: Predict the selected value
sections.content:
| Expression | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `"Ada" or "guest"` | `"Ada"` | First operand is true |
| `"" or "guest"` | `"guest"` | Empty string is false |
| `0 and expensive()` | `0` | First operand is false; call is skipped |
| `[] and "ready"` | `[]` | Empty list is false |

sections.title: Preserve a valid zero
Trace before running
sections.content: For `cache.get(key) or load(key)`, ask whether every false cached value means “missing.” If an empty list is a valid cached result, test membership or a sentinel instead so `load` is not called again.

questions.question: How does Python evaluate chained comparisons and mixed Boolean expressions?
questions.title: Chained Comparisons and Boolean Precedence in Python
questions.direct_answer: Python chains comparisons such as `low < value <= high` as a combined condition with the middle expression evaluated once. For mixed expressions, comparison operators bind more tightly than `not`, then `and`, then `or`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can parse an expression correctly instead of relying on visual intuition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming chained equality compares all values as one group, or reading `and` and `or` with equal precedence.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain single evaluation of the middle comparison expression and use parentheses to communicate intent.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Group an expression using Python's rules, then simplify it into explicit conditions without changing how often its operands run.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `low < value <= high` means both comparisons must hold, and `value` is evaluated once.
Comparison operators have higher precedence than Boolean `not`, `and`, and `or`.
Among Boolean operators, precedence is `not`, then `and`, then `or`.
Chained comparisons test adjacent pairs; `a == b == c` is not the same as `(a == b) == c`.
Use parentheses when grouping is important to the reader, even when precedence already gives the same result.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python reads `low < value <= high` as two adjacent comparisons that must both hold: `low < value` and `value <= high`. It does not compare the first Boolean result with `high`. This notation is strongest when the pairs express one relationship, such as a range or an ordered sequence.

The shared middle expression is evaluated once. In `a < create_value() < c`, Python keeps that returned value for both comparisons, and it skips the second comparison when the first one fails. Rewriting the chain as two comparisons with two calls can change its cost and even its result when the function has state or side effects.

Comparisons bind more tightly than Boolean operators. Among the Boolean operators, the order is `not`, then `and`, then `or`. Therefore `ready or admin and active` means `ready or (admin and active)`. Precedence creates the expression tree first; short-circuiting then decides which parts of that tree actually run.

`a == b == c` means `a == b and b == c`, with `b` evaluated once. It is not `(a == b) == c`, and it does not test whether all three names have one identity. Each adjacent equality still uses the objects' normal `==` rules.

Parentheses are valuable even when Python's precedence already gives the intended result. `is_owner or (is_admin and is_active)` exposes the authorization rule and survives later editing better than a visually ambiguous expression. For larger validation rules, named Boolean values make each condition and its failure case easier to test without changing evaluation order.

This notation is strongest when the pairs express one relationship, such as a range or an ordered sequence.

support.title: One middle call and two Boolean groupings
support.code:
calls = 0

def current_value():
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return 7

print(1 < current_value() <= 10, calls)

ready = False
admin = True
active = False
print(ready or admin and active)
print(ready or (admin and not active))
support.caption: The comparison chain calls `current_value()` once; the final expressions show how grouping changes the policy.

beats.cue: Distinguish a chain from nested Boolean comparison
beats.spokenText: `a == b == c` means `a == b and b == c`, with `b` evaluated once. It is not `(a == b) == c`, and it does not test whether all three names have one identity. Each adjacent equality still uses the objects' normal `==` rules.

beats.cue: Use grouping that communicates the business rule
beats.spokenText: Parentheses are valuable even when Python's precedence already gives the intended result. `is_owner or (is_admin and is_active)` exposes the authorization rule and survives later editing better than a visually ambiguous expression. For larger validation rules, named Boolean values make each condition and its failure case easier to test without changing evaluation order.

sections.title: Parsing happens before evaluation
sections.content:
Precedence decides the expression tree; it does not mean every higher-precedence operation always runs first across short-circuit boundaries. Once grouped, `and`, `or`, and a failed comparison chain can still skip later expressions.

A comparison chain shares adjacent operands. In `a < create_value() < c`, `create_value()` runs once, its result participates in both comparisons, and the second comparison runs only if the first succeeds. Rewriting the expression by repeating the function call could change both performance and behavior.

Parentheses are therefore about grouping, while temporary variables can also control repeated work and give important conditions a name.

sections.title: Trace `low < value <= high`
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  V[Evaluate value once] --> C1{low < value?}
  C1 -- No --> F[Whole chain is False]
  C1 -- Yes --> C2{value <= high?}
  C2 -- Yes --> T[Whole chain is True]
  C2 -- No --> F
```

sections.title: Boolean grouping
sections.content:
| Expression | Effective grouping |
|---|---|
| `not done and valid` | `(not done) and valid` |
| `ready or admin and active` | `ready or (admin and active)` |
| `low < x <= high` | `low < x and x <= high`, with one `x` evaluation |
| `a == b == c` | `a == b and b == c`, with one `b` evaluation |

sections.title: Observe single evaluation and precedence
sections.content:
```python
calls = 0

def current_value():
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return 7

in_range = 1 < current_value() <= 10
print(in_range, calls) # True 1

ready = False
admin = True
active = False
print(ready or admin and active)       # False
print((ready or admin) and active)     # False
print(ready or (admin and not active)) # True
```

The named variables make it easy to test alternative states and verify the intended policy grouping.

sections.title: Rewrite without changing meaning
sections.content: Rewrite `0 <= index < len(items) and items[index] == target` as two named conditions only if you preserve the guard: evaluating `items[index]` before confirming the range could raise `IndexError`.

questions.question: What is the difference between /, //, and % in Python?
questions.title: Division, Floor Division, and Modulo in Python
questions.direct_answer: `/` performs true division, `//` returns the quotient rounded down toward negative infinity, and `%` returns the paired remainder so that `a == (a // b) * b + (a % b)`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Python's floor semantics, especially with negative operands.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `//` as truncation toward zero or expecting Python's remainder to match languages with truncating division.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the quotient-remainder identity to derive negative cases rather than memorizing isolated outputs.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Choose the operation from the required result and correctly trace negative values using Python's floor rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `a / b` is true division; integer operands produce a floating-point result.
`a // b` is floor division; it rounds the quotient down, not toward zero.
`a % b` is the remainder paired with floor division.
For ordinary numeric values, `a == (a // b) * b + a % b` links quotient and remainder.
Division or modulo by numeric zero raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`/` performs true division. Even with two integer operands, it returns a floating-point quotient, so `7 / 3` is about `2.3333`. Use it when the fractional ratio matters, such as an average or a rate, and remember that a numeric zero divisor raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

`//` performs floor division: it rounds the mathematical quotient down toward negative infinity. Positive inputs can make this look like truncation because `7 // 3` is `2`. The negative case reveals the rule: `-7 // 3` is `-3`, while `int(-7 / 3)` truncates toward zero and returns `-2`.

`%` returns the remainder paired with that floor quotient. For ordinary numeric values, `a == (a // b) * b + (a % b)`. Once `-7 // 3` is known to be `-3`, the remainder must be `2` because `-7 == (-3 * 3) + 2`. With nonzero integers, the remainder has the divisor's sign or is zero.

Use `//` and `%` together when a total becomes complete groups plus a leftover. For `155` minutes, the quotient gives `2` complete hours and the remainder gives `35` minutes. `divmod(155, 60)` returns that same pair and makes it explicit that the two numbers come from one division.

Choose `/` for a real quotient and choose `//` with `%` for a floor-based grouping model. Negative inputs deserve an explicit test whenever the domain permits them. Floating-point operands can add rounding edge cases, so quotient-remainder reasoning is clearest with integers and a nonzero divisor.

beats.spokenText: `/` performs true division. Even with two integer operands, it returns a floating-point quotient, so `7 / 3` is about `2.3333`. Use it when the fractional ratio matters, such as an average or a rate, and remember that a numeric zero divisor raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

beats.spokenText: `//` performs floor division: it rounds the mathematical quotient down toward negative infinity. Positive inputs can make this look like truncation because `7 // 3` is `2`. The negative case reveals the rule: `-7 // 3` is `-3`, while `int(-7 / 3)` truncates toward zero and returns `-2`.

beats.cue: Connect modulo to the floor quotient

Once `-7 // 3` is known to be `-3`, the remainder must be `2` because `-7 == (-3 * 3) + 2`. With nonzero integers, the remainder has the divisor's sign or is zero.

beats.recallRule: `/` keeps the ratio, `//` floors the quotient, and `%` supplies the remainder that reconstructs the dividend.

sections.title: One division, three useful results
sections.content:
True division answers “what is the numeric ratio?” Floor division answers “which lower integer bucket contains the quotient?” Modulo answers “what remainder completes that floor-based decomposition?”

The floor rule matters for indexing repeating ranges, time arithmetic, coordinates, and pagination that may cross zero. With a positive divisor, Python modulo gives a result from zero up to but not including the divisor, even when the dividend is negative. This makes expressions such as `index % size` useful for wrap-around.

For integers, `divmod(a, b)` returns the same pair as `(a // b, a % b)` and states that the two results belong together.

sections.title: Derive `-7 // 3` and `-7 % 3`
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R["real quotient: -7 / 3 = -2.333..."] --> F["floor down to -3"]
  F --> Q["quotient = -3"]
  Q --> M["remainder = -7 - (-3 × 3) = 2"]
  M --> I["check: -7 = -3 × 3 + 2"]
```

sections.title: Compare the operators
sections.content:
| Expression | Result | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `7 / 3` | `2.333...` | True quotient |
| `7 // 3` | `2` | Floor quotient |
| `7 % 3` | `1` | Remainder paired with quotient 2 |
| `-7 // 3` | `-3` | Floor, not truncation |
| `-7 % 3` | `2` | Completes `-7 = -3*3 + 2` |

sections.title: Split a duration and verify negative arithmetic
sections.content:
```python
def hours_and_minutes(total_minutes):
    return divmod(total_minutes, 60)

print(hours_and_minutes(155)) # (2, 35)

a, b = -7, 3
quotient, remainder = divmod(a, b)
print(quotient, remainder)              # -3 2
print(a == quotient * b + remainder)    # True
print(int(a / b), a // b)               # -2 -3
```

sections.title: Use the identity
sections.content: To predict `7 // -3` and `7 % -3`, floor the quotient to `-3`, then solve `7 = (-3 * -3) + remainder`. The remainder is `-2`, matching the negative divisor's sign.

questions.question: How do you debug a Python condition that treats a valid value as missing?
questions.title: Debugging Truthiness and Missing Values in Python
questions.direct_answer: Inspect the value, type, and intended meaning of “missing.” A truthiness check groups `None`, zero, `False`, and empty containers together, so use an explicit sentinel or comparison when those values differ.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish absence from falsiness and preserve valid boundary values.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `if not value` or `value or default` without deciding whether zero, false, or empty data is valid.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define the data states first, then use `is None`, membership, or a unique sentinel to encode them precisely.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Turn an ambiguous false branch into explicit states and choose a condition that keeps those states separate.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Log or inspect both `repr(value)` and `type(value)` at the failing boundary.
`None`, `False`, numeric zero, and empty containers are all false in Boolean context.
Use `is None` when absence is the only state that should trigger the branch.
Use key membership when a missing mapping key differs from a stored false value.
Use a unique sentinel object when `None` itself is valid data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python Boolean context treats `None`, `False`, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty collections as false. A custom object can also be false through `__bool__` or a zero `__len__`. That grouping is useful only when the application genuinely considers all of those states equivalent.

At the failing boundary, inspect both `repr(value)` and `type(value)`, then write down which state is supposed to mean missing. Replace a broad `if not value` only after that contract is clear. Use `value is None` when `None` alone represents absence, and use an explicit length or equality check when empty or zero has its own meaning.

An API timeout of `0` might deliberately mean do not wait. `payload.get("timeout") or 30` silently turns that valid zero into `30` because zero is false. Read the value and apply the default only to the agreed missing state. The same problem appears when an empty cached result or an explicit `False` setting is valid data.

A mapping's `get` can make an omitted key and a key storing `None` look the same. Test `"timeout" in payload` when membership is the real question, or pass a unique sentinel object as the default. Because only that object is identical to itself, `value is MISSING` represents omission without taking meaning away from `None`, zero, or `False`.

After choosing the precise condition, test every state the data contract distinguishes: omission, `None`, zero, `False`, empty, and a normal value where they apply. The fix is complete when each state reaches its intended branch, not merely when the first failing example passes. If the states need different outcomes, one truthiness check cannot represent the rule.

sections.title: Truthiness is a category, not a data contract
sections.content:
Boolean context is convenient when the application genuinely cares about empty versus non-empty or enabled versus disabled. It is too broad when the domain distinguishes several false values.

Start by listing the states. An optional count might have `None` for unknown, `0` for known empty, and a positive number for present data. An optional Boolean might have `None` for unanswered, `False` for no, and `True` for yes. Collapsing either field with `if not value` removes information.

A unique sentinel creates an additional identity-based state. Because only the code's sentinel object is identical to itself, it can distinguish an omitted value even when `None` is a valid supplied value.

sections.title: Choose a precise condition
States commonly collapsed by `if not value`
sections.content:
| Value | Truth value | Possible domain meaning | Precise check |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `None` | False | Missing or unknown | `value is None` |
| `0` | False | Valid zero count or timeout | `value == 0` |
| `False` | False | Explicit negative answer | `value is False` when identity is intended |
| `""` | False | Supplied empty text | `value == ""` |
| `[]` | False | Supplied empty collection | `len(value) == 0` |

sections.title: Keep missing, zero, and explicit None separate
sections.content:
```python
MISSING = object()

def timeout_from(payload):
    value = payload.get("timeout", MISSING)
    if value is MISSING:
        return 30       # key omitted
    if value is None:
        return None     # explicit unlimited mode
    return value        # preserves 0

for sample in ({}, {"timeout": None}, {"timeout": 0}, {"timeout": 5}):
    print(timeout_from(sample))
# 30, None, 0, 5
```

The sentinel represents omission, so neither `None` nor zero has to be overloaded as “missing.”

sections.title: Write the state table first
sections.content: Before changing `if not results`, decide whether an empty result means success with no matches, a failed query, or missing data. The correct condition follows that contract and may require a separate status rather than a different operator.
